author: tom
title: Exported talent: almost a quarter of the women's world top 100 were born in China
seo_title: Chinese-born players in table tennis's world top 100
description: Eleven checked where every player in table tennis's world top 100 was born. 24 women and 11 men are Chinese-born, and those abroad are getting older.
standfirst: Eleven traced the birthplace of every player in the latest world ranking. China's influence reaches far beyond its own team, but the generation that left in the 2000s is ageing and the route out is changing.
body: Nine of the 32 women in the singles draw at [WTT Champions Montpellier](/events/wtt-champions-montpellier-2026.html) this week were born in China. Only six of them play for China. Han Ying, the 43-year-old German defender from Shenyang, was drawn to play Romania's Elizabeta Samara on Tuesday evening. Jia Nan Yuan, born in Zhengzhou and in France since she was 18, meets Germany's Sabine Winter on Wednesday, and Australia's Yangzi Liu, from Henan, plays Lily Zhang of the United States on Thursday.

It is a small version of a pattern that runs through the whole world ranking, and it raises a simple question: how many of the world's best table tennis players are Chinese-born, and how many of those represent somewhere else?

Eleven went through the [ITTF world ranking](/rankings.html) published on 26 October and looked up where every player in the top 100 was born. In the women's list, 24 of the 100 were born in mainland China: the 13 who play for China and 11 who represent another association. Those 11 are spread across nine of them: Germany, France, Portugal, Australia, Canada, Singapore, Monaco, the Netherlands and Macau. The men's list is different. China has 10 players in the top 100, and only one more China-born man makes it, Slovakia's Wang Yang, who was born in Anhui.

Eleven counted a player only when a published profile (an encyclopaedia entry, or an Olympic or Commonwealth Games team page) places their birth in mainland China. Players born in Hong Kong were not counted, and nor were a few whose birthplace we could not confirm, so 24 and 11 are minimum figures.

The reason players leave has not changed much in decades. China produces more good players than its national team can use, and a player who is not in the top handful at home can still be among the best in the world elsewhere. Kai Zhang, a China-born player who was trying to make the US Olympic team, put the trade-off plainly in a USA Table Tennis interview quoted by the Associated Press in 2016: "If you want to be a world champion, it is better to train in China." The same AP report quoted an association official, identified only by his surname, Wang, who said "it is in China that they acquired their skills and tactics".

The sport's governing body has tried to slow the flow. In February 2008 the ITTF board voted 46 to 2 to restrict players who switch associations, with Hong Kong and New Zealand against, according to a Xinhua report. Players over 21 who changed would be barred from the World Championships and World Cup for their new country unless they had been resident there, and younger players faced waiting periods of up to seven years. "This showed me that all the member associations know what's the best for the development of table tennis," Adham Sharara, then the ITTF president, said after the vote.

The rule landed just as the exodus peaked. Gijsbert Oonk and Alexander Oonk counted every table tennis Olympian from 1988 to 2020 for a [2023 study in The International Journal of the History of Sport](https://pure.eur.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/97972644/This_Is_Not_a_Problem_but_an_Issue_Chinese_Born_Table_Tennis_Players_Representing_Another_Country_at_the_Olympics_1988_2020.pdf). They found 127 China-born players who represented countries other than China. The number rose to 48 at the Beijing Games in 2008, then fell to 24 at Tokyo. Of the 127, 86 were women.

Today's ranking points the same way. The 11 China-born women in the top 100 who represent other associations have a median age of 38. Seven of them are 37 or older: Portugal's Fu Yu is 47, Han Ying and Germany's Shan Xiaona are 43, the Netherlands' Li Jie is 42, Jia Nan Yuan 41, Monaco's Xiaoxin Yang 38 and Canada's Mo Zhang 37. Only two are under 30: Singapore's Zeng Jian, 29, and Liu, 24. Wang Yang, the only China-born man playing for another country in the top 100, is 32.

Two of the oldest left as teenagers, years before the 2008 rule took effect. Han Ying was 19 when she left China and began playing for the German club TV Busenbach in 2002, and Jia Nan Yuan moved to France in 2003, at 18. Shao Jieni joined a club in Gondomar, Portugal, in 2010, at 16, and Zeng Jian registered with Singapore's association in 2014.

Liu's route shows what the rules now cost a younger player. She moved first to Portugal, settled in Australia in 2019 and became a citizen in March 2020, at 17. Two years later she won a Commonwealth Games singles bronze in Birmingham, Australia's first medal in that event, but under the ITTF's waiting period she was not eligible for the Paris Olympics. "Maybe I have to wait a few more years before I can play Olympics and World Cups and World Championships," she told reporters in 2022, the Canberra Times reported.

Zhu Yuling took a different road. Born in Mianyang, Sichuan, she stepped away from competition in the early 2020s because of health problems, went back to school and later became a teacher, then came back in 2024 for Macau, which has its own association. She is now ranked 11th in the world. "Macao table tennis is relatively unknown internationally," she told Macao News in January.

There is now a route that needs no new passport. Fang Bo, 34, registered this year to play WTT events for Kazakhstan, in partnership with the Nomad Table Tennis Academy, the South China Morning Post reported. He said he would not play the Olympics, World Championships or World Cup. "I still hold Chinese nationality," he wrote on social media.

So the question for the next decade is who replaces the generation of Han, Fu and Jia. If fewer young Chinese players settle abroad, the associations that have relied on them will need to develop more of their own. For now, three of the women carrying the exported game into the [Montpellier draw](/news/montpellier-draw-lebrun-sun-yingsha-2026.html) are 24, 41 and 43, and only two of the 11 in the top 100 are under 30.
